t.landscape of the pico island vineyard cu:
The vines on Pico grow in a basalt maze. For five hundred years, the islanders have built tiny walled enclosures called currais out of black volcanic stone, each one just big enough for a few vines, to protect the plants from salt wind and sea spray, and the result is a landscape of thousands of small rectangles covering the rough coastal lava plain, mile after mile, with parallel walls running down toward the sea. UNESCO listed this vineyard culture in 2004, and the sight of it from the coastal road is among the strangest and most beautiful in Europe. The grapes ripen in the heat that the black stone holds, and the wines, especially the white Verdelho, were once shipped to the courts of the Russian tsars.

Pico is the second largest island of the Azores and is dominated by the volcano that gives it its name, the highest mountain in Portugal at 2,351 metres, its upper slopes often hidden in cloud. In the nineteenth century, disease destroyed most of the vines, and the culture shrank, but in recent decades it has been revived, and new wines are winning prizes. The coast has a whaling history, too: the men of Pico hunted sperm whales from open boats until the 1980s, and the museum at Lajes do Pico tells the story. Today the same waters are famous for whale-watching.

Madalena, the town where the ferry from Faial arrives, has about six thousand people and the fuel, shops and restaurants you need. The ride around the island, on the ring road that hugs the coast, is a series of long bends between stone walls, hydrangea hedges and black cliffs, with the occasional detour up to a crater lake or a lava cave. Surfaces are generally good, but the weather is the issue. Azorean weather can change in minutes, with wind, rain and fog, and the volcano's summit is seldom clear.

The best time is from May to September, when the days are long and mild. Hydrangeas bloom in July and August, lining the roads in blue. Winter is wet and stormy.

Try the local cheese, queijo do Pico, and the island's limpets, lapas, grilled with garlic and butter. They go well with a glass of Verdelho.
t.dhaka@23.8,90.4:
Everything here moves at once: rickshaws painted with bright murals, green CNG autorickshaws, buses with dented flanks, cars, cargo bikes and pedestrians, all swarming through the same space with a kind of fluid logic.

The city sits on the Buriganga River, and its history is longer than its modern chaos suggests. Dhaka was a Mughal provincial capital in the seventeenth century, and from that period come the Lalbagh Fort, an unfinished palace complex with a gentle garden and a tomb, and the pink Ahsan Manzil, the riverside palace of the Nawabs of Dhaka. The old city's narrow lanes are full of brass workers, bookbinders, sweet shops and some of the best street food in South Asia, including kacchi biryani and bakarkhani bread. Dhaka is also famous for its muslin cloth, once so fine that it could be drawn through a ring, and for its enormous fleet of cycle-rickshaws.

Be realistic about riding here. Traffic is intense, rules are flexible, and a foreign rider will need local knowledge, a good deal of patience and probably a local guide. Roads flood in the monsoon, and the pollution can be heavy in winter. Think carefully about licences, insurance and permission to bring a vehicle, and consider hiring a local bike with a driver for the city part.

The long day described here heads southwest toward Bagerhat, where the Sixty Dome Mosque and other fifteenth-century monuments built by the saint-governor Khan Jahan Ali stand among ponds and palm trees, inscribed as a UNESCO site in 1985. The route crosses the great rivers of the Ganges delta, and the Padma Bridge, which opened in 2022, has made the trip dramatically quicker than the old ferry crossing. Fuel is easy to find in and around Dhaka, but start early to beat the traffic.

If you can, finish with tea on a rooftop or a river cruise at dusk, when the city's noise is softened by the light.
t.part ii@38.6,-28.4:
Pico is an island that is mostly mountain. The great cone of Mount Pico rises to about 2,350 metres from the Atlantic, the highest point in Portugal, and its slopes sweep down in black lava to the sea. The summit, often wrapped in cloud, appears from nearly everywhere on the island and from the neighbouring island of Faial, and climbing it is a long, steep day on loose volcanic rock, with an extraordinary view if the weather behaves.

The label belongs to a UNESCO listing, the Landscape of the Pico Island Vineyard Culture, which protects an extraordinary agricultural invention. On the island's lava fields, the early settlers could not plough, so they built thousands of small enclosures, curraletas, from black basalt stones, and planted vines inside them to shelter from wind and salt spray. The result is a labyrinth of tiny walled plots stretching down to the sea, which makes a strange and beautiful pattern from above. The vines produce Verdelho, a white wine that was once drunk at the courts of Europe, and the tradition is still alive.

The island's other great story is whaling. For more than a century, men from Pico hunted sperm whales from open rowing boats, using hand harpoons, and the white lookout huts on the hills and the whale-oil factories still stand. The Whalers' Museum at Lajes do Pico tells the story, and whale-watching boats now take visitors to see the animals without harpoons. The last hunt took place in the 1980s.

For riding, the roads that circle the island are a pleasure. The coastal road passes through villages of black stone houses with white trim, past hedges of blue hydrangeas, and the views of the sea and of Faial across the channel are superb. The surface is generally good, with long curves and some tight bends, and the traffic is light. Wind and rain can arrive rapidly, and fog on the high roads can cut visibility. Take care on wet basalt and on cattle that cross unannounced.

Fuel is available in Madalena, the main town, about eleven kilometres away, and in São Roque and Lajes, so fill up there before you go. Cafes and small restaurants serve grilled limpets, fresh fish and local cheese, and the meat stews are famous.

The best months are from May to September, but the weather can change in minutes at any time. A ferry from Madalena to Horta, on Faial, takes about thirty minutes.
t.deadhorse@70.2,-148.5:
Deadhorse is not a town in the usual sense. It is an industrial camp at the end of the Dalton Highway, a place of warehouses, trucks, workers' lodges and a single general store, serving the Prudhoe Bay oil field on the Arctic coastal plain of Alaska. About 414 miles of gravel and dirt road run north from Fairbanks, crossing the Yukon River, the Arctic Circle and the Brooks Range at Atigun Pass before the land flattens into tundra, and the whole way the Trans-Alaska Pipeline snakes beside you, sometimes above ground on its zigzag supports, sometimes buried.

The last stretch from Coldfoot is about 240 miles with very little in the way of services. Fuel is sold at Coldfoot and again here, but nowhere reliable between except the tiny community of Wiseman, so riders carry spare fuel and plan carefully. The road is mostly gravel, sometimes rough, treated with dust control that turns to slick mud in the rain, with heavy trucks that dominate the road. Give them room, ride with lights on, and expect stones thrown up by passing vehicles. Tyres, spare tubes and tools are not optional.

The landscape is the real reward. North of the Brooks Range the land spreads out in huge, flat expanses of tundra, with caribou, muskoxen, and in summer a carpet of small flowers. The sun does not set for weeks in midsummer, so riding at midnight is possible, and in winter it vanishes entirely. Mosquitoes in July can be savage, and weather can turn quickly from sunny to freezing rain, so bring layers and waterproofs.

Visitors need to know that Deadhorse sits inside a working oil field, and access to the Arctic Ocean itself is controlled. Independent travellers usually book a shuttle tour for the last few miles to the shore. Rooms and meals are available at a few lodges but are expensive and often full, so book ahead. The permanent population is only a few hundred, with workers rotating in from elsewhere. The best months are June to August, after the road has dried and before the snow returns.
t.vista do rei@37.8,-25.8:
Everyone who rides on São Miguel eventually ends up at this lay-by, and they all take the same photograph. Vista do Rei looks down into the caldera of Sete Cidades from its western rim, and what you see is a giant green bowl with two lakes lying side by side in the bottom, one blue and one green, a pretty village between them and a neat white church with its spire. The viewpoint takes its name from King Carlos I, who is said to have admired the view on a royal visit at the start of the twentieth century.

Behind you stands a half-ruined building that was once meant to be a grand hotel, never quite finished and now sitting in the weeds with its empty windows. It has become part of the place, and in cloud it looks properly haunted. On the other side of the road hydrangeas form long blue and pink hedges in July and August, flowering so thickly that the road feels like a corridor of flowers.

The weather up here deserves respect. The Azores are famous for having four seasons in a day, and the rim of the crater collects cloud like a bowl collects soup. You can arrive in sunshine and find the lakes gone, then wait ten minutes and watch them reappear. Patience pays, and so does an early start, before the tour buses and the afternoon mist. The ride along the rim is lovely: smooth tarmac with good grip when dry, easy bends, grass and cows on the shoulders, and mild gradients. Watch for wet surfaces and sudden fog, and give the cattle plenty of room.

Do not expect services here. There is a small stand sometimes selling drinks, but food, fuel and a proper stop are better found elsewhere. Ponta Delgada, the capital, is about twenty-five minutes' ride away and has everything, while the smaller villages of Mosteiros and São Vicente have basic shops. Fill the tank before you climb, because distances in the west of the island are longer than they look on the map.

The Azores sit on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and the lakes occupy an old volcanic crater, which is why the landscape feels so tidy and so wild at once. Linger a little, listen for wind and cowbells, and let the clouds decide when to open.
t.sete cidades@37.9,-25.8:
Down at the bottom of the caldera, the view from the rim turns into something more intimate. The village of Sete Cidades sits on a narrow strip of land between two lakes, the Lagoa Azul and the Lagoa Verde, which are joined by a short channel and a little bridge. A neo-Gothic church, São Nicolau, stands among small houses, with a lane leading off to the water, and the whole place smells of wet grass, woodsmoke and cows.

The local legend is a love story, as legends should be. A princess fell in love with a shepherd, and when her father the king forbade them to meet, they said goodbye by the water; the princess's eyes were blue and the shepherd's green, and their tears filled the two lakes. Scientists prefer the explanation that algae and the reflection of sky and surrounding hills produce the difference, but the story is told with a straight face to every visitor. The lakes lie in a volcanic crater about five kilometres across, formed in an eruption long ago, and the surrounding walls are steep and green with forest and farm.

The road down from the rim is a treat, a narrow twisting descent with cobbled edges, hydrangea hedges and good views at every bend. It is mostly smooth, though patchy in places, and slick after rain, so take it gently. Cars and buses come the other way and the lanes are narrow, which makes a motorcycle the right tool. Early morning is best, when the water is still and the mist drifts across the surface.

Down in the village there are a few small cafés and snack bars, where a coffee and a cake called a queijada are about right. The local dairy tradition is strong, and cheese is worth buying to carry in your pannier if you have space. There are walking trails around the lakes and up to the rim, but do not underestimate how steep the climb back is on foot.

Ponta Delgada is the sensible place to fill up, and Mosteiros has a small shop but not much else. Allow time here for slow sipping and strolling, because the mood is more peaceful than almost anywhere else on the island.
t.mosteiros@37.9,-25.8:
Mosteiros sits at the very western tip of São Miguel, where the road runs out of island and the Atlantic takes over. It is a small village of low houses, a harbour, a church and an old basalt shoreline, and the reason people come is the group of sea stacks standing just off the coast. They are black, jagged and covered with the green of lichen and salt-hardy plants, and they look like the ruins of something. The name means monasteries, and one story says that the stacks resemble the shapes of monks' cowls, though the origin of the name is not entirely clear.

The shoreline is volcanic through and through. Dark sand and polished stones form a small beach, and a natural pool among the lava rocks is a lovely place to swim on a calm day. When the sea is rough, you can feel the swell thumping into the rock before you see it, and spray flies over the sea wall. It is wise to read the water before you wade in, and to stay away from the edge in heavy surf, as the Atlantic here can be unforgiving.

The ride in is an easy descent from Sete Cidades through green fields and small stone-walled farms. The road is mostly smooth with steady bends, though cattle, tractors and wet leaves are all potential hazards, and the sea fog sometimes drifts in over the lanes. The light in late afternoon turns the cliffs golden, and the sunsets facing west are a good reason to linger. The village smells of salt, fish and baking, and local cafés serve simple fish dishes, cheese, and strong coffee.

Do not expect more than a few shops and snack bars. For fuel, you need to go to larger places, and the nearest sizeable town is Arrifes, though Ponta Delgada has the widest range, roughly half an hour east. A tank filled before you come west is a good idea. Weather can change fast, and wind off the sea is cold even in July, so a spare layer is useful.

There is also a quiet sadness in the end of the road: after the dramatic crater you have just left, this is where the island simply meets the horizon, and there is nothing between you and America.
t.ponta delgada@37.7,-25.7:
Ponta Delgada is the main town of the Azores, on the south coast of São Miguel, a green volcanic island in the middle of the Atlantic. The town is laid out along the sea, with black basalt and white limestone pavements in patterns that make the streets look like a drawing, and three big arches, the Portas da Cidade, mark the old entrance from the harbour. Fishing boats, whale-watching boats and ferries come and go, and the island's wealth once came from oranges, then pineapples, which are still grown in glasshouses and are sold in the market with a sweetness you will not forget.

Outside town the island is a lesson in volcanoes. West of Ponta Delgada the road climbs to the rim of Sete Cidades, a huge caldera holding two lakes side by side, one blue and one green, with a village on the shore and hydrangea hedges along the road in summer. East, the Lagoa do Fogo sits in a crater high in the middle, and further on the valley of Furnas has hot springs, steaming vents and a stew, the cozido, cooked underground in the volcanic heat. The oldest tea plantation in Europe, at Gorreana on the north coast, still produces tea on the hillside, and you can walk through the rows.

The riding is very good, and also very wet. The roads wind up and down the volcanic slopes between stone walls, cattle pastures and forests of cedar and Japanese cryptomeria, with tight bends and sharp gradients, and the views change with each ridge. Cloud can drop to the road in minutes, and the island is famous for having four seasons in a day, so a waterproof layer is not optional. Cows are moved along the roads by farmers, and slow vehicles, sudden fog and wet cobbles in villages are the hazards. Spring and early autumn are comfortable, and summer is warmer and busier, especially in August.

Ponta Delgada, with about twenty thousand people in the town itself, has all the fuel, food and services you need, and stations are spaced around the island but not in every village. Fill up before you head to the remote crater roads. Try fresh grilled limpets with garlic and butter, a local treat, and a slice of the island's cheese, and finish with a coffee on the waterfront.
t.buffer zone 3@38.4,-28.4:
Pico Island rises out of the Atlantic in the central Azores as a single enormous volcano, and its summit, at about 2,351 metres, is the highest point in Portugal. It is a country of black lava, small stone-walled fields and a sea that is always close, with the great cone usually wrapped in cloud above you.

The vineyards are the island's most remarkable feature. Over centuries, farmers cleared the harsh, rough basalt and used the stones to build thousands of tiny walled plots, called currais, to shelter vines from salt wind and sea spray. The result is a grid of black stone rectangles running down to the shoreline, with small windmills and old stone houses among them, and it is recognised as a World Heritage landscape. The wine made here, particularly the white Verdelho, was exported to the courts of Europe, including, so the story goes, the Russian tsars, in the nineteenth century, until disease destroyed most of the vines. The work of the vineyards is still done mostly by hand.

The riding is slow, rewarding and deeply different from the mainland. The ring road runs around the island, with tight bends, short climbs and sudden views of the sea and the neighbouring island of Faial, and a series of smaller roads climbs from the coast toward the mountain through pasture and forest of Japanese cedar and laurel. Rain and fog come quickly, and the black basalt is slippery when wet, so keep your speed down in villages where the road is paved with old cobbles. Cows are herded along the roads, and the verges are lined with hydrangeas in summer.

Madalena, the largest town on the island, has fuel, shops and a ferry connection to Faial, and São Roque and Cais do Pico have basics. The stations can be far apart on the quieter sides of the island, so top up when you pass one. Fresh fish, limpets and the island's sweet bread are the local pleasures, and a glass of local wine in a small tavern is easy to find.
t.part i@38.6,-28.4:
Part I belongs to the protected vineyard landscape of Pico, the Azorean island dominated by a single volcano, and it lies on the northern side, between Cais do Pico and São Roque, with Madalena a bit further west. It is the other face of the island from the sunny southern slopes, a coast where the sea beats against black rock, the cloud sits low on the pasture, and the fields are small and green. The place is best understood as part of a long strip of cultivated lava running along the shore.

What you see here is the work of generations. Early settlers, who arrived in the fifteenth century, found fresh lava fields with little soil, and they broke the stone, piled it into walls and filled the gaps with whatever earth they could collect, creating small walled enclosures where vines could survive the salt wind. In places the old wine cellars and tanks, made of dark volcanic stone, stand by the shore, and small harbours, such as those for hauling barrels and boats, are cut into the lava. Whaling was also a Pico tradition, with lookout huts on the hills and open boats rowed out to hunt sperm whales until the 1980s, and the old whaling museum at São Roque tells that story. Today the same waters are used for whale-watching, and the animals can be seen on many days in summer.

Riding here, you follow narrow roads between stone walls, with the mountain behind and the sea in front, and a mix of village streets and short climbs. The surface is generally good, but there are many sharp bends, and mist can cut visibility to a few metres on the higher slopes. Dry weather is more common in summer, though showers pass through at any time, and the light after rain is spectacular, with the mountain suddenly emerging from the cloud. On a clear day, you may see the whole cone and, across the water, the island of São Jorge as a long line on the horizon.

Cais do Pico and São Roque are small towns with basic shops and cafes, and fuel is available in the larger settlements. Madalena has the best selection, so plan ahead.
